extracted.intended_audience: general readers of 19th-century travel literature and people interested in Saharan travel, ethnography, and practical observations about Timbuctoo and Ghat
extracted.subtask_short: travelogue chapter on Ghat and Timbuctoo
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter from a 19th‑century travelogue describing daily life, customs, practical preparations, routes, and agricultural/irrigation practices around Ghat and accounts of Timbuctoo. Contains observational prescriptions and procedural descriptions relevant to travel and local practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrigation as the foundation of Saharan agriculture
rubrics_metrics.description: Irrigation is the grand means of agricultural production in Sahara; without irrigation the oases would be mere halting-places and would afford but a scanty supply for centres of human existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical method described: water is drawn from wells (by bullock or slave), poured into a receiver, then into small earthen conduits; fields are divided into small squares/compartments (~seven by five feet) edged with small embankments; a lad opens each compartment to admit water and shuts it when the surface is covered. Irrigation is repeated every four or five days (in Ghat) until grain is in ear and nearly ripe. Main conduits sometimes made of lime-mortar; water-raising and distribution is central to productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical caravan/camel management for Saharan travel
rubrics_metrics.description: Strings of camels are tied one after another, held together by strings in their nose; camels are not allowed to graze during the march, and files of camels are typically twenty or thirty in number (sometimes double).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not allowing camels to graze is presented as an advantage to the traveller because it saves time lost by camels cropping herbage. In mountainous districts camels may be untied to avoid one camel slipping and dragging the line into confusion. These organizational details are given as practical norms for caravan travel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Route and safety considerations for travelling to Timbuctoo / Fezzan
rubrics_metrics.description: There are multiple routes; southern (south-western) route to Timbuctoo is variously estimated (map: forty-five days; Sheikh: thirty days or less). The route is intersected by many high mountains (attract rain) but includes the 'dreaded plain of Tenezrouft' — eight days without water for man or herbage for camels, the grand difficulty in getting to Timbuctoo from the north.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Travel security advice is implicit: plan according to local estimates of travel time, be aware of waterless stretches (Tenezrouft), and seek trustworthy guides (e.g., Jabour's promise to conduct en route). The author stresses difficulty of getting there and back as the main hazard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical packing and handling of senna for trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Senna packing: originally packed in Aheer sacks which may wear out and are repacked locally; sacks are made of palm-leaves; senna leaves vary by season (finer and broader after rains) and contain small wood stalks, a few yellow flowers, and dust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing senna for market: inspect and, if necessary, change worn sacks; note seasonal quality differences in leaves; be aware of contaminants (stalks, dust). These are presented as routine trade/practical steps rather than formal standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social/hospitality norm: feeding/provisioning visiting Touaricks
rubrics_metrics.description: When Touaricks (foraging parties) arrive demanding food, the prudent merchant shares supper to avoid conflict: 'the supper which Haj Ibrahim had prepared for himself, was brought out to them... And like a wise steward, he kept a little back for his lord and master.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antipattern: parsimony or refusing to share provokes disorder. Guidance implied: offering provisions to hungry/travelling Touaricks (or the local protectors) is a pragmatic way to maintain peace in the Souk and avoid trouble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual sensitivity: avoid introducing religious discussion in certain public markets
rubrics_metrics.description: The author reproved merchants for introducing the subject of religion before the ignorant people of Ghat and Soudan, asking 'If they would do so in Tripoli, and if not, why here?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative guidance: avoid proselytizing or initiating religious debates in contexts where it is inappropriate or inflammatory (e.g., local souks), especially when one would not do the same in one's own home city. This is presented as a practical rule to prevent unrest or offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fashion/hairdressing practices for Libyo‑Saharan women
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed prescription of fashionable hair-dressing: forehead shaved high leaving one long curl ('with') braided and hanging over the forehead; three double-braided curls on each side over the ears; two longer curls behind the head double-braided; crown area shaved clean except small tuft; hair rubbed with olive-oil or daubed with semen or liquid butter; finished hair forms an oval crown shape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stepwise procedure: shave specified areas, gather and braid curls in tiers, rub with oily substance, tie ends with coloured string/ribbon. The author frames this as an established local toilette practice and notes perfunctory social context (daily grooming, professional hairdresser).

rubrics_metrics.name: Material culture notes: women's dress and adornment norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical dress: a chemise and short‑sleeved frock, with a barracan used as a shawl over head/shoulders; sandals or shoes; beads prized mainly by Negresses (Venetian/Trieste clay beads fashionable); Touarick women prefer coral and charms; arms/wrists/ankles hooped with painted wood and metal armlets; some wear small looking-glasses on a neck string.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are descriptive standards for regional female dress and ornamentation useful to observers and traders; also notes changing textile consumption (introduction of cheap European 'Indians' cottons supplanting Soudan cottons) as a commercial/cultural consideration.
